module_title: Section 138: Dishonour of Cheques & Recent Amendments
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, Judiciary, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the most heavily litigated section in Indian commercial law: Section 138. It dissects the strict procedural timeline required to file a criminal case for a bounced cheque and covers the crucial 2018 amendments regarding interim compensation.

core_concepts.title: Section 138: The Crime of Dishonour
core_concepts.description:
Bouncing a cheque is a criminal offence under the NIA. It is punishable with imprisonment up to **2 years**, or a fine which may extend to **twice the amount of the cheque**, or both.
- Core Rule: The cheque must have been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. (A cheque given as a 'gift' bouncing does NOT attract Section 138).

core_concepts.title: The Strict Timeline of Section 138
core_concepts.description:
To successfully prosecute, this strict mathematical sequence MUST be followed:
1. Presentation: The cheque must be presented to the bank within **3 months** from the date it is drawn (validity period).
2. Dishonour: The bank returns it unpaid (usually due to 'insufficient funds' or 'stop payment').
3. Demand Notice: The payee must send a legal notice demanding payment within **30 days** of receiving the return memo from the bank.
4. Grace Period: The drawer is given **15 days** from the receipt of the notice to make the payment.
5. Filing the Complaint: If the drawer fails to pay within those 15 days, the cause of action arises. The payee must file the criminal complaint in court within **30 days** from the expiry of the 15-day grace period.

core_concepts.title: Presumptions in Favour of the Holder (Sec 118 & 139)
core_concepts.description:
Criminal law usually presumes innocence, but NIA creates 'Reverse Burdens'.
- Section 139: The court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received it for the discharge of a debt or liability.
- Burden of Proof: The accused drawer has to prove that the cheque was NOT issued for a debt (e.g., proving it was stolen or lost as a blank security cheque). The burden is heavy.

core_concepts.title: The 2018 Amendments (Sections 143A & 148)
core_concepts.description:
Introduced to stop drawers from intentionally delaying trials.
- Section 143A (Trial Stage): The trial court can order the drawer to pay Interim Compensation to the complainant up to **20% of the cheque amount** while the trial is still ongoing. If the drawer is acquitted, the complainant must refund it with interest.
- Section 148 (Appellate Stage): If the drawer is convicted and appeals, the appellate court can order the drawer to deposit a minimum of **20% of the fine/compensation** awarded by the trial court as a condition for hearing the appeal.

important_entities.name: Offences by Companies (Section 141)
important_entities.key_fact: Directors are vicariously liable for corporate cheques.
important_entities.significance: If the person committing a Section 138 offence is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business (like the Managing Director) shall be deemed guilty. They can escape liability only by proving they had no knowledge or exercised due diligence.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Drawers often argue: 'The cheque didn't bounce for insufficient funds, it bounced because I issued a Stop Payment instruction to the bank. Therefore, Section 138 doesn't apply.' **FALSE**. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a 'Stop Payment' instruction, 'Account Closed', or 'Signature Mismatch' still attracts Section 138 if the underlying reason was avoiding a legally enforceable debt.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Validity (3M) -> Notice after bounce (30D) -> Wait for payment (15D) -> File complaint (30D).

exam_strategy_tips: In CLAT PG or Judiciary Mains, when discussing judicial delays in Section 138 cases, you must highlight the **Section 143A (20% interim compensation)** provision as the legislative mechanism intended to curb frivolous litigation.
